items.stem: A client with diabetes becomes diaphoretic and confused. Capillary glucose is 2.8 mmol/L (50 mg/dL). The client is now unconscious and cannot swallow. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Administer glucagon as ordered/protocol because the client cannot safely take oral carbohydrate.
Give orange juice by mouth immediately while the client remains unconscious.
Wait 30 minutes to recheck glucose before any treatment.
Encourage the client to walk briskly to raise blood glucose without medication.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck states adults/children unable to eat or drink can receive glucagon; OpenStax states glucagon may be given IV/IM/SC if the client is unable to eat or drink or is unconscious.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Oral carbohydrate is unsafe in an unconscious client who cannot protect the airway; both sources reserve oral sugar for clients who can eat or drink.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize prompt treatment of hypoglycemia; delaying risks worsening neurologic injury.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Exercise does not treat severe hypoglycemia and delays definitive glucose/glucagon therapy.

items.stem: A community nurse finds an older adult with sudden right-arm weakness, facial droop, and slurred speech that began 20 minutes ago. Complete the bowtie: identify the priority condition, two nursing actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Stable essential hypertension without acute neurologic change

actions.text: Activate emergency medical services immediately (call for ambulance/911-equivalent)
Note the time symptoms were first noticed
Advise driving privately to a clinic appointment tomorrow
Have the client take a long nap before seeking care
Apply ice to the face and wait for speech to improve overnight

parameters.text: Airway patency and ability to protect the airway
Level of consciousness and evolving neurologic deficits
Shoe size for future footwear shopping

rationales.K1: Correct. Sudden unilateral weakness, facial droop, and speech difficulty are classic stroke signs (CDC); Merck notes diagnosis is suggested by sudden neurologic deficits.
rationales.K2: Incorrect. Ankle sprain does not explain acute facial droop and speech change.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Chronic stable hypertension alone does not explain new focal deficits.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Cerumen impaction does not cause acute hemiparesis and dysarthria.
rationales.A1: Correct. CDC advises calling emergency services right away and not driving privately so treatment can begin en route.
rationales.A2: Correct. CDC states noting the time symptoms first appear helps determine treatment eligibility; time-sensitive care is emphasized.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Delaying care overnight/to tomorrow risks missing time-limited stroke therapies.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Sleeping instead of emergency activation delays reperfusion opportunities.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Ice and watchful waiting are inappropriate for suspected stroke.
rationales.P1: Correct. Airway protection is a primary safety priority while awaiting/en route to emergency care.
rationales.P2: Correct. Evolving neurologic status/consciousness must be monitored as stroke can progress (Merck clinical assessment).
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Entertainment preferences are irrelevant emergency parameters.
rationales.P4: Incorrect. Shoe size is not an acute stroke monitoring parameter.
rationales.P5: Incorrect. Food preferences are not priority stroke parameters.

items.stem: A client with a tibial fracture reports severe leg pain that seems worse than expected for the injury and intensifies when the nurse passively stretches the toes. Distal pulses are still palpable. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Compartment syndrome — notify the provider urgently because pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are early cues.
A normal healing response that never requires provider notification while pulses remain present.
Only anxiety, so analgesics can be deferred indefinitely without reassessment.
Isolated cerumen impaction unrelated to the injured limb.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: earliest symptom is pain out of proportion, exacerbated by passive stretch; treat before pallor/pulselessness. OpenStax lists pain out of proportion worsened by passive stretch among the five Ps and requires urgent provider notification.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Intact pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome; Merck notes perfusion can fail before pulses disappear.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Disproportionate pain after fracture is a surgical emergency cue, not reassurance that anxiety alone explains findings.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Ear findings are unrelated to limb compartment ischemia.

items.stem: While changing a dressing on postoperative day 5 after abdominal surgery, the nurse sees bowel protruding through a fully separated incision. Which action is correct?

options.text: Cover the exposed bowel with a sterile dressing moistened with sterile saline, position to reduce wound tension (e.g., low Fowler’s with knees slightly flexed), keep NPO, and notify the surgeon immediately.
Push the bowel firmly back into the abdomen with clean bare hands and send the client home.
Leave the wound uncovered and encourage coughing exercises to “work the bowel back in.”
Apply a dry nonsterile towel from the bathroom and schedule routine follow-up in 2 weeks.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: medical emergency — low Fowler’s, sterile towel soaked with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride, notify provider, remain NPO. StatPearls: wrap bowel in gauze moistened with warm saline and prepare for emergent exploration.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Forcing reduction with bare hands is unsafe and delays sterile protection and surgical care.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Leaving bowel exposed and encouraging cough increases injury/desiccation risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nonsterile delayed follow-up is inappropriate for evisceration, a surgical emergency.

items.stem: A community health nurse is counselling a healthy 72-year-old client before influenza season. Which teaching point is accurate?

options.text: An annual influenza vaccine is recommended because adults 65 years and older are at higher risk for serious flu complications.
Influenza vaccine is unnecessary after age 65 because older adults no longer benefit from immunization.
One childhood influenza vaccine provides lifelong immunity, so boosters are never needed.
Only people under age 18 should receive influenza vaccine.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC states flu vaccination is especially important for people ≥65 because of higher complication risk; Merck states the influenza vaccine should be given annually to eligible patients and notes higher mortality in adults >65.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize vaccination importance in older adults rather than abandoning immunization.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Merck and CDC frame influenza immunization as an annual need due to antigenic change/seasonal risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Adults, especially those ≥65, are a priority group for influenza vaccination.

items.stem: A public health nurse teaches families about everyday hand hygiene. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash hands with soap and clean running water before preparing food and before eating.
Wash hands after using the toilet and after changing diapers.
Wash hands after blowing the nose, coughing, or sneezing.
Skip handwashing after handling garbage because household trash is sterile.
If soap and water are not available, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.
Avoid washing hands after touching animals or animal waste.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC lists before/during/after food preparation and before eating as key times; OpenStax Microbiology restates CDC food-related key times.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC and OpenStax include after toileting and after diaper changes.
rationales.C: Correct. CDC and OpenStax include after coughing, sneezing, or blowing the nose.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC lists after touching garbage as a key time to wash hands.
rationales.E: Correct. CDC advises alcohol-based sanitizer with ≥60% alcohol when soap and water are not available.
rationales.F: Incorrect. CDC and OpenStax include after interacting with animals/animal waste as a key time.

items.stem: An emergency department triage nurse has two waiting clients: one with sudden crushing chest pain and diaphoresis, and one with an isolated ankle injury who is stable and in moderate pain. Who should be prioritized first and why?

options.text: The client with chest pain, because potentially life-threatening cardiopulmonary problems take priority over a painful but non–life-threatening extremity injury.
The client with the ankle injury, because extremity trauma is always more urgent than chest symptoms.
Neither client — triage is unnecessary if both can sit in chairs.
Whoever arrived first, regardless of acuity or ABC priorities.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: chest pain is prioritized before an ankle injury because MI risk is more life-threatening. Merck warns that attending to dramatic but not deadly injuries before immediate life threats can be fatal; primary survey uses ABCDE.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sources prioritize life-threatening conditions over isolated extremity injury.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Triage exists specifically to prioritize by acuity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Arrival order alone ignores ABC/acuity prioritization taught in both sources.

items.stem: During a mass-casualty intake, which statement best reflects correct initial prioritization using the ABCDE approach?

options.text: Assess and address airway first, then breathing and circulation, before less immediate concerns.
Complete a detailed social history interview before checking airway patency.
Ignore breathing problems until after arranging outpatient physiotherapy.
Skip circulation assessment if the client can speak about favourite hobbies.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax ABCDE triage assesses airway first, then breathing and circulation. Merck primary survey uses A-B-C-D-E and begins with systems posing the most immediate threat to life.

rationales.C: Incorrect. Breathing threats are addressed early in ABCDE, not deferred to outpatient planning.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Circulation remains a core primary-survey element even if the client can converse.

items.stem: Complete the teaching for a client newly prescribed digoxin.

ngn.template: Before each dose, the nurse assesses the pulse for 1 minute and withholds digoxin if the heart rate is less than {B1}. The client should report possible toxicity signs such as {B2}.

B2.text: anorexia, nausea/vomiting, and visual changes (e.g., yellow-green halos)
improved appetite with no other symptoms

rationales.B1a: Correct. OpenStax: assess pulse 1 minute; do not administer if HR <60.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. 120 bpm is not the OpenStax withhold threshold for digoxin.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. 200 bpm is not the nursing withhold parameter taught for digoxin.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Respiratory rate is not the digoxin pre-dose pulse withhold criterion.
rationales.B2a: Correct. OpenStax lists anorexia, nausea, vomiting, visual changes/halos; Merck lists nausea, vomiting, anorexia and serious arrhythmias among toxic effects.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Improved appetite alone is not a toxicity warning cluster.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Toenail growth is unrelated to digoxin toxicity monitoring.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Furniture rearrangement is not a digoxin toxicity cue.

items.stem: An adolescent with sickle cell disease presents with a severe vaso-occlusive pain crisis. Which nursing plan is most appropriate initially?

options.text: Provide prompt analgesia (often IV opioids as ordered) and maintain hydration (IV fluids as ordered), while monitoring oxygenation.
Withhold all pain medication until laboratory cultures return in 48 hours.
Encourage prolonged fasting without fluids to “dry out” sickled cells.
Discharge immediately without analgesia because pain crises are never treated in hospital.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: analgesics (usually opioids) and IV hydration are mainstays for vaso-occlusive pain crisis; oxygen if hypoxic. OpenStax: acute crisis may require IV fluid replacement and analgesics (predominantly IV opioids).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delaying analgesia for routine culture wait is not supported; pain treatment is central.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Dehydration precipitates/worsens sickling; both sources emphasize hydration.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Both sources describe hospital management with fluids and analgesia for acute crises.

items.stem: A client in a cast develops increasing pain out of proportion to injury and pain with passive stretch. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated now.

rows.text: Notify the provider/rapid response pathway immediately for suspected compartment syndrome.
Continue frequent neurovascular assessments of the affected limb.
Apply a tighter circumferential bandage over the cast to “reduce swelling space.”
Assume intact distal pulses mean compartment syndrome is impossible and document only “reassured.”

rationales.R1: Indicated. OpenStax: appearance of five-P findings is urgent — notify provider immediately. Merck: diagnosis/treatment must occur before pallor/pulselessness; treatment is fasciotomy.
rationales.R2: Indicated. OpenStax emphasizes frequent assessment of the at-risk limb; Merck stresses clinical vigilance for evolving ischemia.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Tight circumferential devices can worsen compartment pressure (Merck lists tight bandages/casts among causes).
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Merck notes cellular perfusion can stop before pulses disappear; intact pulses do not exclude the diagnosis.

items.stem: After caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea, which hand hygiene action is correct?

options.text: Wash hands with soap and water rather than relying on alcohol-based sanitizer alone.
Use only alcohol-based sanitizer because soap never removes C. difficile spores.
Skip hand hygiene if gloves were worn at any point.
Rinse hands with sterile water only, without soap, after every C. difficile contact.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax states C. difficile is an example of organisms not removed by hand sanitizers and requires soap and water. CDC states washing with soap and water is the best way to remove germs in most situations.
rationales.B: Incorrect. OpenStax explicitly advises soap and water rather than sanitizer for C. difficile.
rationales.C: Incorrect. OpenStax requires hand hygiene after glove removal; gloves do not replace hand hygiene.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Soap (with water) is required; water alone is not the recommended method.
